title: attention is the only thing you actually own
hook: attention is the only thing you actually own
tomorrow: the rule that keeps turning up

segments.voice: Two words in. Breathe, and sit. Your line was sit anyway. Did you manage one breath of waiting without reaching for anything? Or did the pull win? Both tell you something. Day three.

Think about what's asking for your attention right now. The screen in your hand. A notification you haven't opened. Something someone said this morning that you're still turning over. Whole companies are built to win a few more seconds of it, and they're very good at their jobs. You can lose money and earn it back. You can lose a day, and there's another one tomorrow. But the thing you're spending, all day long, is attention. Today starts with a bold claim: attention is the only thing you actually own. Let's see if it holds up. Today's word is notice.
screen: `WHAT'S ASKING FOR YOU RIGHT NOW?` → `EVERYONE WANTS A FEW SECONDS.` → `THE THING YOU'RE SPENDING.`

segments.voice: In 1890 the American psychologist William James published a huge book, The Principles of Psychology. In the chapter on attention he wrote a line that sounds simple and isn't: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Not what happens to you. What you attend to. Two people can sit through the same dinner and go home with two different evenings, because they noticed different things. James also saw that attention wanders, all the time, and that bringing it back is the real skill. He wrote that "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." Over and over again. Not once. That matters, because most people who try to pay attention think the wandering means they failed. For James, the coming back was the whole thing. Buddhism has a word for this, from Pali, the language of its early texts: sati. It's usually translated mindfulness, but it comes from a root that means to remember. Remembering to come back to what's here. Buddhist teachers build a whole path of practice around it. And the Greek teacher Epictetus, who was born enslaved, taught his students to sort everything into two piles: what's up to us, and what isn't. Your body, your reputation, what other people do: not up to you, he said. Your own judgments and choices: up to you. Three voices, three different reasons, and none of them needs the others. So, is attention really the only thing you own? Maybe not the only thing. But it may be the one you can take back fastest. You just did, by listening.
screen: `WHAT I AGREE TO ATTEND TO.` · `BRINGING IT BACK, OVER AND OVER.` · `SATI: REMEMBERING TO COME BACK.` · `WHAT'S UP TO US, AND WHAT ISN'T.` · then, large: `THE ONE YOU CAN TAKE BACK FASTEST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first breath, notice one thing you can hear. Just one. On the second breath, notice one thing you can feel: your feet, the seat, the air on your skin. On the third breath, notice where your attention went just now. Did it wander? Good. You noticed. That's the whole practice: the coming back.
Notice. To see what's already here, and to see where your mind just went. Third word.
Your line: where is it right now? Three times today, ask it quietly: where is my attention right now? Don't fix the answer. Just notice it, and bring it home. Day three.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY PATH ON EARTH ARRIVED AT IT ON ITS OWN.`

howItsDone: Buddhist mindfulness practice trains attention by resting it on something simple, often the breath, and gently bringing it back each time it wanders; many other traditions use a word, a sound or a candle flame the same way.

what a scholar hears: James 1890, chapter XI, defines attention as "the taking possession by the mind" of one of several possible trains of thought. Pali sati comes from the same root as Sanskrit smṛti, memory.
